subject: Communication
title: The Door-in-the-Face Technique
description: A fast breakdown of The Door-in-the-Face Technique for builders.

hook.text: 'Volunteer every weekend for two years?' No way. 'How about just this Saturday?' That sounds fair.

buildup.text: Door-in-the-face is the opposite of foot-in-the-door: start with an absurd request, then retreat to the real one.

discovery.text: Cialdini showed that the retreat triggers reciprocity — 'I lowered my ask, so you should meet me halfway.'

twist.text: The first request was never real. It existed only to make the second request seem like a concession.

climax.text: Negotiators, fundraisers, and salespeople use this daily. The 'unreasonable' ask is always calculated.

punchline.text: Sometimes the real ask hides behind the ridiculous one.

quiz.question: How does the door-in-the-face technique work?
options: Start big, retreat to the real request

details.summary: The door-in-the-face technique begins with an extreme request designed to be refused, followed by a moderate one that seems reasonable by comparison. The contrast effect and reciprocal concession make the second request hard to refuse.
details.whyItMatters: This technique is used in negotiations, fundraising, and diplomacy. Recognizing the pattern prevents you from anchoring to an inflated starting point.
takeaways: Start with an extreme request to make the real one seem small
Contrast effect shifts the perception of reasonableness
Reciprocal concession pressures the other party to compromise

faq.question: When does the door-in-the-face technique fail?
faq.answer: It fails when the initial request is so extreme that it seems absurd or insulting, breaking rapport. It also fails if there is too long a delay between the two requests, or if a different person makes the second request, eliminating the concession dynamic.

faq.question: How is this different from anchoring in negotiation?
faq.answer: Anchoring sets a reference point that pulls estimates toward it. Door-in-the-face specifically uses rejection of the first offer to create a sense of obligation through reciprocal concession. Anchoring influences perception; door-in-the-face leverages social pressure.
